entities.name: Dartmouth College
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Dartmouth College, founded in 1769 in Hanover, New Hampshire, is the smallest of the eight Ivy League institutions and the last colonial college founded before the American Revolution. Originally established to educate Native Americans alongside English youth — its charter specified 'the education and instruction of Youth of the Indian Tribes in this Land' — Dartmouth achieved fame from its 1819 Supreme Court case Dartmouth College v. Woodward, which established the principle that private corporations' charters cannot be revised by state legislatures.

Dartmouth was founded by Eleazar Wheelock, who received a royal charter from King George III to educate indigenous peoples. The Native American educational mission was largely unrealized — few Native Americans attended; the institution served primarily English colonists. However, Dartmouth's symbolic Native American identity persisted through its 'Indian' mascot until 1969, when the college under President John Sloan Dickey retired the mascot and began actively recruiting Native American students.

The Dartmouth College case (1819) — in which Daniel Webster argued before the Supreme Court to preserve Dartmouth's private charter against New Hampshire's attempt to convert it to a public university — established that corporate charters are contracts protected by the Constitution. Chief Justice John Marshall's ruling became a foundational precedent in American corporate law, protecting private institutions from state interference. The ruling helped legitimize American private enterprise and the independence of private educational institutions.
